name: Commentary on and misreadings of the METR update

author_credentials: METR authors: staff of METR, an AI-evaluation nonprofit; Becker, Rush and Rein co-wrote the 2025 trial. Rob Bowley: software practitioner blogging at 'Adventures In Software Development'; no credentials stated on the post. His closing 'take' favours strong engineering practices, which is his professional theme. Birchtree: personal blog, tagline 'Developer and creator'; a tech link-blogger, not a researcher. Sebastian Mondragon: writes for Particula Tech, a consultancy; the post ends by selling 'Particula Tech's AI tooling audits', so it has a commercial interest in readers distrusting borrowed numbers. Eric D. Brown, D.Sc.: consultant (site lists Services); commercial interest in advising on AI measurement. TFD: pseudonymous forum author, no affiliation given. AgentMarketCap and CoderCops: vendor/market blogs with a commercial interest in the coding-agent market. braindetox.kr and urandom.io: no author credentials found. No commentary by a named economist or academic software-engineering researcher was found.

exact_quotes.quote: Our raw results show some evidence for speedup. Our early 2025 study found the use of AI causes tasks to take 19% longer, with a confidence interval between +2% and +39%. For the subset of the original developers who participated in the later study, we now estimate a speedup of -18% with a confidence interval between -38% and +9%. Among newly-recruited developers the estimated speedup is -4%, with a confidence interval between -15% and +9%.

we believe that the data from our new experiment gives us an unreliable signal of the current productivity effect of AI tools. The primary reason is that we have observed a significant increase in developers choosing not to participate in the study because they do not wish to work without AI, which likely biases downwards our estimate of AI-assisted speedup.

Based on conversations with study participants, we believe it is likely that developers are more sped up from AI tools now — in early 2026 — compared to our estimates from early 2025. However, because of the selection effects in our experiment, our data is only very weak evidence for the size of this increase.

exact_quotes.source: METR, section 'Wider adoption of AI has made it more difficult to measure task-level productivity'
exact_quotes.quote: An increased share of developers say they would not want to do 50% of their work without AI, even though our study pays them $50/hour to work on tasks of their own choosing.
When surveyed, 30% to 50% of developers told us that they were choosing not to submit some tasks because they did not want to do them without AI.

Together, these effects make it likely that our estimate reported above is a lower-bound on the true productivity effects of AI on these developers. The selection effects seem to affect a minority share of developers and of tasks, which limits the degree of bias.

Based on our interviews and surveys we believe the increase in selection is primarily due to higher expectation of AI-driven uplift by our developers. However the second study also had a lower pay rate, $50/hour instead of $150/hour in the original study, and this also likely contributed to the higher selection.
Altogether, these issues make it challenging to interpret our central estimate, and we believe it is likely a bad proxy for the real productivity impact of AI tools on these developers.

Please interpret these results with a major grain of salt, due to this increased selection, and see the blog post for further detail.
You may be seeing posts claiming METR's widely-cited 2025 study has been followed up with new research showing an 18% productivity boost. That's not what the article says.

The interesting part is why the study broke down. Developers are now so reliant on AI that they won't work without it (to be part of the control group). And the nature of how they work when using GenAI has changed too, which undermines e.g. simple time-on-task measurements.

METR believe GenAI coding productivity is improving – but say they can no longer measure it reliably with this study design and are reworking their approach. Personally I don't see how you can practically design an effective controlled experiment considering everyone uses it now.

these kinds of studies are still a narrow window on software delivery – individual task completion by autonomous open-source contributors, not developers working in teams on production codebases with all the organisational complexity that entails.
Additionally, while they don't have conclusive results, their early findings seem to indicate that the uptick in productivity is actually pretty significant now.
their original study was of developers using Claude Sonnet 3.5 through cursor while this new study would've been using Claude Code with Opus 4.5

METR's 2026 point estimate for the returning developers was a "speedup" of -18%. In METR's signed notation, a negative speedup is a slowdown. The number barely moved: from about -19% in 2025 to -18% in 2026, essentially flat.

exact_quotes.source: Particula Tech, section 'Did METR reverse its 19% slowdown finding in 2026?'
exact_quotes.quote: So the "37-point swing" and "18% speedup" you may have seen are artifacts of reading -18% as +18%.

exact_quotes.source: Eric D. Brown, 3 Mar 2026, section 'What Happened at METR'
exact_quotes.quote: The new results showed the opposite: an 18% speedup for returning developers. The researchers themselves flagged the new data as unreliable.
Between the two studies, developers started refusing to participate in tasks where AI wasn't allowed. Thirty to fifty percent declined to submit tasks they wouldn't attempt without AI.
When I obtain an estimate for the entire sample that METR makes available I get a sample-wide estimated speedup of 6%.

exact_quotes.quote: negative values indicate speedups
for the subset of original developers who returned, the estimate flipped to an 18% speedup. For new recruits, a 4% speedup. But METR is clear the data is weak.
Because METR did not define the mathematical sign convention for speedup, juxtaposing these verbatim expressions without asserting a single interpretation preserves factual accuracy.

key_claims: WHAT METR'S TEXT SAYS. (a) The new experiment gives 'an unreliable signal'. (b) The raw results 'show some evidence for speedup': returning developers -18% (CI -38% to +9%), new recruits -4% (CI -15% to +9%). (c) METR believes developers are likely more sped up in early 2026 than early 2025, on the basis of conversations with participants, and calls its own data 'only very weak evidence for the size of this increase'. (d) The estimate is likely a lower bound and 'a bad proxy'. (e) Selection affects 'a minority share of developers and of tasks'. (f) The pay cut 'also likely contributed'. THE SIGN. -18% is a speed-up: tasks took an estimated 18% less time with AI allowed. Three things in METR's own material settle it. The same paragraph gives the 2025 result as tasks taking '19% longer' with an interval of +2% to +39%, so positive means more time. The paragraph opens 'Our raw results show some evidence for speedup', and the next sentence says the true speedup 'could be much higher'. METR's published regression.py computes the figure as exp(beta) - 1, where beta is the coefficient on the AI-allowed dummy in a regression of log implementation time. A negative value means less time with AI. METR's phrase 'a speedup of -18%' is loose wording for a -18% change in time, and it is what caused the confusion. WHO READ IT AS A SPEED-UP (correct on sign): Eric Brown ('an 18% speedup for returning developers'), urandom.io ('flipped to an 18% speedup'), AgentMarketCap ('a speedup of 18%'), CoderCops ('roughly 18% faster'), and TFD, who re-ran METR's public data and got a 6% to 7% sample-wide speed-up, noting 'negative values indicate speedups'. Most of these add that METR flagged the number as unreliable. WHO READ IT AS A SLOWDOWN (wrong on sign): Particula Tech (Mondragon) says 'a negative speedup is a slowdown', that the 2025 figure was 'about -19%' and that the estimate was 'essentially flat'. This contradicts METR's +2% to +39% interval for 2025 and METR's 'some evidence for speedup'. braindetox reports, without naming them, that one Korean-language blog printed '18% slowdown, -9% to +38%' and another paired 'slowdown' with the original interval. WHO DECLINED TO READ A DIRECTION: Rob Bowley does not call -18% a slowdown. He says posts claiming 'an 18% productivity boost' misrepresent an article whose point is that the data is too compromised to use, and he accepts that 'METR believe GenAI coding productivity is improving'. braindetox says the sign is ambiguous because METR gave no formula (it did not check the public regression script). Birchtree quotes no number; it says early findings 'seem to indicate that the uptick in productivity is actually pretty significant now'. WHERE COMMENTATORS GO BEYOND METR. Bowley: 'Developers are now so reliant on AI that they won't work without it' and 'everyone uses it now'. METR's text is narrower: 30% to 50% withheld some tasks, an 'increased share' would not do half their work without AI, and selection affects a minority. METR never uses 'reliant' or 'dependent'; it attributes the behaviour to 'higher expectation of AI-driven uplift' plus lower pay. Bowley does not mention the pay cut. Bowley also says METR 'couldn't complete' the experiment; METR says the data is unreliable and that it is changing the design, and it published 800+ tasks of data. Birchtree: 'pretty significant' overstates 'only very weak evidence', and the claim that the new study used 'Claude Code with Opus 4.5' is not in METR's post, which names only 'agentic tools ... such as Claude Code and Codex'. Eric Brown: developers 'started refusing to participate in tasks where AI wasn't allowed' and 'the refusal is the data point' is his interpretation; he omits the pay cut. Particula: 'refused to run the no-AI arm' and 'refused to do the no-AI half of the experiment' misdescribe what METR reports, which is tasks not being submitted before randomisation.
headline_figures: -18%: METR, 'we now estimate a speedup of -18% with a confidence interval between -38% and +9%', for the 10 developers from the original study who joined the later one; AI-allowed vs AI-disallowed tasks; study began August 2025, post dated 24 Feb 2026. Means 18% less time with AI. Interval includes zero.
-4%: METR, 'Among newly-recruited developers the estimated speedup is -4%, with a confidence interval between -15% and +9%'; 47 new developers. Interval includes zero.

+19%: METR, 'Our early 2025 study found the use of AI causes tasks to take 19% longer, with a confidence interval between +2% and +39%'; data February to June 2025. The post's first sentence rounds this to 'a 20% slowdown'.

30% to 50%: METR, 'When surveyed, 30% to 50% of developers told us that they were choosing not to submit some tasks because they did not want to do them without AI.' Share of surveyed developers, about some tasks. No survey n or question wording given.
$150/hr to $50/hr: METR, 'we reduced the pay from $150/hr to $50/hr'.
57 developers, 143 repos, 800+ tasks; 10 returning and 47 new; median 10 years' experience (METR, 'Details of the productivity study').
'18% productivity boost': Rob Bowley's wording for the claim he is rebutting, 4 Apr 2026. Not METR's wording.

6% (whole sample), 7% (mixed model), 12% (tasks expected to be much faster with AI), 25% (best single developer), 20% (heuristic 'synthetic' figure): TFD's reanalysis of METR's public data, 14 Mar 2026, all speed-ups. TFD says the 20% deliberately leans high and is not a best guess.

'about -19% in 2025 to -18% in 2026, essentially flat' and '37-point swing' is a misread: Particula Tech, 2 Jul 2026. Wrong: the 2025 figure is +19% in the same convention, so the point estimates differ by about 37 points in time-change terms.
'18% speedup' / '18% faster': Eric Brown (3 Mar 2026), urandom.io (1 Mar 2026), AgentMarketCap (5 Apr 2026), CoderCops (1 Aug 2026), all for returning developers.
sample_and_method: Not a study. A reading of METR's 24 Feb 2026 post and its public regression script against nine pieces of commentary published 1 Mar to 29 Sep 2026, found by web search and opened directly. The underlying METR experiment is randomised at the task level (AI-allowed vs AI-disallowed), with developers choosing which tasks to submit before randomisation; 57 open-source developers, 800+ tasks, from August 2025. None of the commentators collected data except TFD, who re-ran regressions on METR's published data.csv. The commentary sample is whatever search surfaced; it is not a systematic survey of reactions.
evidence_offered: METR: its own regression estimates, participant surveys and interviews, and three developer quotes. Bowley: METR's post, plus CircleCI's 2026 State of Software Delivery report for his system-level point; no new data and no figures quoted from METR. Birchtree: one quoted METR paragraph and personal experience of the tools. Particula: quotes from METR's post, read with the wrong sign. Eric Brown: METR's figures and one developer quote. TFD: regressions on METR's public dataset. The others restate METR.
data_vintage: METR post published 24 Feb 2026; experiment began August 2025; no end date given in the post, and the repo README still has a literal placeholder ('occured during DATE'). 2025 comparison data: February to June 2025. Commentary dated 1 Mar 2026 (urandom.io), 3 Mar (Brown), 14 Mar (TFD), 4 Apr (Bowley), 5 Apr (AgentMarketCap), 29 Jun (Birchtree), 2 Jul (Particula), 1 Aug (CoderCops), 29 Sep (braindetox). METR page text read on 12 Oct 2026; no revision notice on it.
figure_provenance: -18%, -4%, 30% to 50%, the pay rates and the 57/143/800+ counts all originate in METR's 24 Feb 2026 post; there is no paper. Conflicting versions in circulation: (1) '18% speedup' or '18% faster' (Brown, urandom.io, AgentMarketCap, CoderCops), right on direction but often quoted without the interval; (2) '18% slowdown' (Particula; unnamed Korean-language blogs per braindetox), wrong; (3) '18% productivity boost' (Bowley's description of others' posts); (4) AgentMarketCap prints 'a speedup of 18%' with the interval '-38% to +9%', mixing conventions; (5) the 2025 figure appears as both '19% longer' and '20% slowdown' inside METR's own post; (6) TFD's 6% to 7% whole-sample figure is a third-party rerun of METR's pooled data, not a METR figure, and METR's post reports no pooled estimate. 'Developers refused to work without AI' is a paraphrase that appears in Bowley, Brown and Particula; METR's wording is that they chose not to participate, or not to submit some tasks.
population_and_transfer: Experienced open-source developers (median 10 years) paid $50/hour to work on their own projects, choosing their own tasks. Transfer to salaried engineers in ordinary companies is weak: Bowley makes this point himself ('individual task completion by autonomous open-source contributors, not developers working in teams on production codebases'). Employees cannot usually withhold tasks from their employer, so the selection mechanism is specific to a voluntary paid study.
outcome_measured: Task speed (self-recorded implementation time per task, AI-allowed vs AI-disallowed). The 30% to 50% figure is a self-report about task submission. The commentary measures nothing; it interprets.
limitations_stated: METR: 'unreliable signal'; 'only very weak evidence for the size of this increase'; 'likely a bad proxy for the real productivity impact'; self-reported speedups 'can be quite unreliable'; time measurements 'unreliable for the fraction of developers who use multiple AI agents concurrently'; selection 'primarily due to higher expectation of AI-driven uplift' but lower pay 'also likely contributed'. Repo README: 'interpret these results with a major grain of salt'. Bowley: such studies are 'a narrow window on software delivery'. Birchtree: 'they don't have conclusive results'. TFD: the heuristic 'can't truly "correct" for any selection' and 'None of these numbers should be taken as my personal best-guess'. Particula and Brown state no limits on their own readings.
counter_evidence: Against the slowdown reading: METR's own sentence 'Our raw results show some evidence for speedup', the +2% to +39% interval attached to '19% longer', the exp(beta) - 1 estimand in regression.py, and TFD's independent rerun giving a speed-up. Against the confident speed-up reading: both intervals include zero (-38% to +9%, -15% to +9%), and METR calls the central estimate a bad proxy. Against 'developers won't work without AI': METR says selection affects 'a minority share of developers and of tasks', gives no count of developers who declined to take part, and names the cut from $150 to $50 an hour as a contributor. Against Bowley's 'I don't see how you can practically design an effective controlled experiment': METR lists six options, including shorter, better-paid experiments, fixed-task experiments and developer-level randomisation, while noting the last worsens developer-level selection and has lower power.
alternative_explanations: The reluctance may be a pay effect: at a third of the earlier rate, fewer developers accept the inconvenience of a no-AI assignment, whatever their attachment to the tools. METR says it believes expectations are the main driver, on interviews and surveys, but gives no decomposition. Preferring AI may be a rational choice about expected time saved; the developer quotes ('AI can finish things in just 2 hours, but I have to spend 20 hours') read that way, and no commentator opened here separates preference from dependence. The move from +19% to -18% among returning developers may reflect ten self-selected people out of the original cohort, better tools, more practice, or noise within overlapping uncertainty. Developers' expectations of uplift were shown to be overoptimistic in the 2025 study, so tasks withheld for 'high expected uplift' need not have high actual uplift; METR asserts the bias runs downward but this is an inference, not a measurement.
verification_status: VERIFIED against the opened primary source: all METR quotes and figures (metr.org page text); the estimand definition (regression.py on GitHub); Bowley's post text and its 4 April 2026 date; Birchtree's post text and its 29 June 2026 date; Particula's slowdown reading and 2 July 2026 date; Eric Brown's text and 3 March 2026 date; TFD's figures and 14 March 2026 date (via a mirror of the EA Forum post); the quoted lines from urandom.io, AgentMarketCap, CoderCops and braindetox. NOT VERIFIED: the Birchtree author's full name (page shows only the handle @matt); which Korean-language blogs printed '18% slowdown' (braindetox does not name them); any METR staff comment on the sign confusion (none found; X/Twitter and LinkedIn not searched directly); a Joel Becker podcast appearance mentioned in a search summary (not found, not opened); METR's later post 'Measuring the Self-Reported Impact of Early-2026 AI on Technical Worker Productivity' (seen only as a card on the METR page: 'A survey of 349 technical workers finds a median 1.4-2x self-reported change in value of work'; not opened, not dated). METR's blog index lists no later post on a redesigned randomised study up to 6 Oct 2026, but the index page was only scanned for titles.
relevance_to_essay: Central as a caution. The update is the main evidence that the no-AI control is getting harder to run, and the commentary shows two opposite ways to get it wrong: reading -18% as a slowdown (Particula), and inflating '30% to 50% withheld some tasks' into 'developers won't work without AI' (Bowley, Brown). The thought should say -18% is a speed-up with an interval that includes zero, and keep METR's own limits: a minority of developers and tasks, one study, and a pay cut.
implications_for_measurement: Commentators draw three lessons, none tested. Bowley: task-time experiments miss team-level delivery, so look at system outcomes (he cites CircleCI on less code reaching production). Brown: stop estimating an AI productivity percentage and track business outcomes before and after. Particula: run your own task-level A/B and enforce the control arm, which is the very thing METR found hard with volunteers, though an employer has more leverage than a study recruiter. METR's own list is more specific: shorter, better-paid experiments; observational data; careful questionnaires with time-use studies; fixed-task experiments; developer-level randomisation with its stated costs. The sign muddle carries its own lesson: report an effect as time change or as speed-up, state which, and give the interval.
open_questions: Whether anyone at METR has publicly corrected the slowdown reading. How many developers declined to take part at all (METR gives no count). The survey question and n behind '30% to 50%'. How much of the selection is pay. Whether any economist or software-engineering academic has published a response; none was found. Which specific posts Bowley was rebutting (he names none). What pooled estimate METR itself would report (only TFD's 6% to 7% rerun exists).
